title: Episode 50: The Honey War of 1839: The Border Feud Over Three Bee Trees
description:
The Honey War of 1839: The Border Feud Over Three Bee Trees: How Missouri and Iowa mobilized armed militias and nearly sparked civil war over delinquent taxes and three hollow bee trees. Join Rebecca and George for an immersive historical deep dive into this extraordinary chapter of the American story.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome back to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Along the winding Des Moines River in the bitter autumn of 1839, two American frontier territories nearly went to shooting war against one another. It was not fought over slavery, federal gold, or major industrial river ports, but over a vague surveying line, a county sheriff attempting to collect delinquent property taxes, and three hollow honeybee trees. Before cooler heads and common sense prevailed, thousands of armed militiamen faced off in waist-deep December snow with swords, squirrel rifles, scythes, horse pistols, and sausage stuffers. Here is George with the full, unbelievable story of the Honey War.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: THE RAPIDS OF THE RIVER DES MOINES
In the early decades of the nineteenth century, the northern boundary of the state of Missouri was defined by an ambiguous Indian treaty that designated the border at the parallel of latitude passing through the rapids of the River Des Moines. However, there was a fatal cartographic ambiguity that would confound surveyors and ignite frontier hostility for more than a generation. In the mighty Mississippi River itself, there were well-known limestone shallows known as the Des Moines Rapids, located where the river tumbled over rock shelves between modern-day Keokuk and Montrose. But ninety miles up the winding Des Moines River proper, there was also a minor, shallow riffle known locally as the Keokuk Rapids. In 1837, the Missouri legislature commissioned a surveyor named John Sullivan to run the boundary line eastward to the Mississippi. Sullivan set out into the wild prairie, but his magnetic compass was deflected by hidden underground mineral deposits and iron deposits in the hills. As a result, Sullivan's survey line bowed dramatically northward into what would soon become Iowa Territory. The resulting disputed wedge of territory, known as the Sullivan Line, was a rich, fertile strip of prime timber, limestone bluffs, and black loam roughly ten miles wide. Hundreds of eager homesteaders poured into this fertile frontier to stake claims, clear timber, and build log cabins, completely unaware of which territorial government held legal authority over their hearths.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE SHERIFF AND THE BEE TREES
The flashpoint of the border controversy arrived in the crisp autumn of 1839 in Van Buren County, Iowa. The sheriff of Clark County, Missouri, a determined and unyielding official named Uriah S. 'Sandy' Gregory, crossed northward into the disputed strip to collect state taxes from the settlers. When the Iowa homesteaders flatly refused to acknowledge Missouri jurisdiction or surrender their hard-earned currency, Sheriff Gregory announced that he would seize their personal property in lieu of payment. Specifically, Gregory located three massive, hollow bee trees belonging to an Iowa settler named Davis. On the frontier, honey was far more than an occasional luxury. In an era before refined cane sugar was widely available in frontier general stores, wild honey was the primary sweetener for cooking, preserving fruits, and baking, as well as a vital trade commodity that could be bartered for flour, gunpowder, and iron tools. Sheriff Gregory brought out his axes, felled the three giant timber trees, and extracted hundreds of pounds of wild golden honeycomb, carting it back across the state line to pay off the delinquent tax bill. To the Iowa pioneer families who had spent months locating the hives and guarding them from black bears, the chopping down of the bee trees was viewed as brazen, government-sanctioned theft. The outraged settlers immediately sent frantic dispatches to Territorial Governor Robert Lucas in Burlington, demanding executive intervention and military protection against Missouri plunderers.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE ARREST OF SANDY GREGORY
Governor Robert Lucas was not a man to brook territorial trespass. A fierce, weathered veteran of the War of 1812 and the former governor of Ohio, Lucas had previously commanded troops during the Toledo War border dispute with Michigan. He instantly issued a blistering proclamation warning Missouri authorities that any further attempts to exercise civil or legal authority on Iowa soil would be treated as an armed foreign invasion. Undaunted by Lucas's fiery rhetoric, Sheriff Sandy Gregory returned to the disputed territory in November 1839, accompanied by a small squad of armed Missouri deputies, determined to levy taxes on additional Iowa homesteaders along the river bottomlands. But this time, the Iowans were lying in wait. Sheriff Henry Heffleman of Van Buren County, backed by a resolute posse of thirty heavily armed pioneer farmers, intercepted Gregory on the muddy dirt wagon road near Farmington. They leveled their rifles, placed Sheriff Gregory under arrest for extortion and illegal trespass, disarmed his men, and transported him northward under heavy guard to the territorial jail in Muscatine. Word of their county sheriff's humiliating capture reached Governor Lilburn Boggs of Missouri in Jefferson City. Boggs, who had already gained national notoriety for issuing the infamous extermination order against Mormons, took the arrest of his county official as an act of open insurrection. Without consulting President Martin Van Buren or waiting for federal mediation, Governor Boggs issued urgent orders to the state militia: mobilize five full divisions and prepare to march north to crush Iowa defiance and enforce the dignity of Missouri.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE ARMIES GATHER IN THE SNOW
In response to Governor Boggs's mobilization, Governor Lucas called out the territorial militia of Iowa, declaring that the sacred soil of the territory must be defended at all costs. More than twelve hundred frontiersmen rallied in southeastern Iowa under the command of Major General Jesse Browne. The assembly was one of the most eccentric and motley military forces ever gathered on the American frontier. Lacking standardized federal weaponry or state uniforms, the Iowa men arrived armed with whatever implements could inflict injury: flintlock muskets from the Revolution, heavy octagon-barrel squirrel rifles, scythes lashed to poles, broadaxes, cavalry sabers, horse pistols, and in one celebrated instance, an oversized tin sausage stuffer carried proudly over the shoulder like a naval blunderbuss. Across the border, the Missouri forces, numbering over a thousand men under General David Willock, encamped in the freezing mud along the Des Moines River. Neither army possessed adequate winter uniforms, wool blankets, canvas tents, or field commissaries. As December temperatures plummeted below zero and a blinding blizzard blanketed the Mississippi valley in knee-deep snow, both armies found themselves shivering violently around smoky campfires. They suffered from acute frostbite and hunger, subsisting on parched corn, roasted venison, and whatever kegs of corn whiskey could be requisitioned from nearby frontier trading posts.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE BALLAD OF THE HONEY WAR
As the two freezing armies glared at each other across the icy river, the utter absurdity of the standoff began to dawn on the rank-and-file soldiers. Many of the settlers on opposite sides of the border had intermarried, traded horses, cleared roads together, and attended each other's barn raisings for years. Frontier humor and frontier common sense began to overcome political posturing. A Missouri satirist and poet named John Campbell composed a widely circulated folk song titled 'The Honey War', which mocked both governors for risking hundreds of human lives over a tub of stolen honey and three rotted hollow trees. The song spread through both military encampments like wildfire, sung aloud around the blazing logs at night. Verses described Governor Boggs summoning mighty heroes to battle for wild bees, while Iowa warriors marched out in ragged wool coats with pitchforks and sausage guns to defend their sacred right to sweet corn cakes. In the Missouri camp, soldiers sliced a haunch of venison, labeled one half Governor Lucas and the other half Governor Boggs, and shot them full of musket balls in mock execution. Laughter and derision began to systematically erode the martial fury of the militia.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE PEACE DELEGATES AND THE TAVERN
Recognizing that their men were freezing to death in the blizzard and harbored no genuine desire to slaughter their neighbors, peace commissioners from both territories secretly convened near the border hamlet of Clark City. A delegation of respected Iowa citizens, bearing flags of truce, entered the Missouri camp just as the Missouri state legislature in Jefferson City passed an emergency resolution urging peace and suspension of military maneuvers. In an extraordinary scene of frontier reconciliation, the commanding officers of both armies met at a crude log tavern. They laid aside their swords, ordered several barrels of rye whiskey, and toasted each other in fraternal harmony, laughing heartily at the pompous declarations of their respective governors. General Jesse Browne of Iowa and General David Willock of Missouri reached an immediate gentleman's agreement: both armies would disband without firing a single hostile shot, and the entire boundary question would be submitted to the Congress and Supreme Court of the United States. Sheriff Sandy Gregory was quietly released from the Muscatine lockup, provided with a warm meal and a horse, and allowed to ride home to his family, bearing no lingering grudges against his Iowa captors.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE SUPREME COURT AND THE GRANITE MARKERS
Ten years after the Honey War, in February 1849, the Supreme Court of the United States finally issued its landmark decision in the case of Missouri versus Iowa. The justices examined historical French and Spanish maps, Indian treaties, the Sullivan survey notes, and the testimony of early river pilots. The Court ruled unanimously in favor of Iowa, holding that the Sullivan Line, as corrected for magnetic variation, represented the true and legal boundary between the two sovereign states. In the summer of 1850, joint boundary commissioners traveled the entire border, erecting massive cast-iron and carved granite monuments every ten miles from the Des Moines River to the Missouri River. Today, the Honey War remains one of the most delightful and celebrated episodes in Midwestern history: a crisis where frontier citizens refused to shed each other's blood over political vanity, proving that common sense, good humor, and shared fellowship could resolve the thorniest territorial disputes of the American frontier.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
The Honey War proved that frontier common sense could triumph over bureaucratic arrogance. The only casualties of the entire campaign were three bee trees and a few stray hogs. I'm Rebecca. Join us next week for another journey through the wild, hidden chapters of our past.
